newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD's Diller says German deficit out of control.
newsitem.headline: SPD's Diller says German deficit out of control.

text.p: Germany's federal deficit in the first two months of 1997 was two-thirds of the level budgeted for the full year, undermining efforts to qualify for European monetary union (EMU), opposition Social Democrat (SPD) budget spokesman Karl Diller said on Monday.

"Chancellor (Helmut Kohl) should come clean on how things are to proceed with Europe," Diller said. "Under this government, Germany stands no chance of meeting the Maastricht goal. Finance Minister (Theo Waigel's) debt policies will make the euro soft."
The federal deficit totalled 34.8 billion marks in January and February, compared with 53.3 billion marks budgeted for the full year, Diller said, citing Finance Ministry data.
"The causes ... include the fact that expenditures are once again totally out of control," Diller said in a statement.

To qualify for the single European currency, Germany aims to cut its total public sector budget deficit to below 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year from 3.9 percent last year. But many economists are sceptical it will succeed.
The data for 1997 are critical because they will form the basis for the decision of what countries participate in EMU from the start.

Waigel aims to cut 1997 government outlays 3.4 percent from last year's level, but in the first two months of the year they were 2.5 percent higher than the same period last year, Diller said. Tax revenues, forecast to rise 2.1 percent for the full year, were down 7.1 percent in the two months, he said.
A supplementary budget is needed to show the real state of affairs and to take the necessary measures to fight unemployment, Diller said.

The Finance Ministry rejected the SPD demand for a supplementary budget, a ministry spokesman said, adding that every year there are extraordinary factors that distort the fiscal picture at the start of the year.
Tax revenues in January and February had developed as foreseen in the government's annual report on the economy, released in late January, the ministry spokesman said.

In Brussels, Waigel said many reasons including reunification, payments to the European Union, aid to eastern Europe and the debts of the Bundesbahn railway were behind the high outstanding level of German debt.
